title: Respiratory control in fresh and stored mitochondria
passage: Isolated mitochondria allow electron transport and ATP synthesis to be studied separately. In a sealed chamber fitted with an oxygen electrode, the rate at which O₂ disappears reports the rate at which electrons reach Complex IV. By adding reagents in a fixed order, investigators can probe one part of the coupled system at a time. One group used this approach to ask how cold storage affects rat liver mitochondria. They compared mitochondria tested within an hour of isolation (fresh) with mitochondria from the same isolation that had been held on ice for 24 hours (stored).

Each run contained 1.0 mg of mitochondrial protein in 2.0 mL of buffer with phosphate and Mg²⁺ at 30 °C. The investigators made five additions in sequence. First came the NADH-linked substrates glutamate and malate (state 2). Next came 200 nmol of ADP (state 3); the fast rate lasted until all of the added ADP had been phosphorylated, and then the rate fell (state 4). Third came oligomycin, an inhibitor of the Fo portion of ATP synthase. Fourth, the protonophore FCCP was titrated to the concentration giving the highest rate. Last came antimycin A, which blocks Complex III. In parallel runs under identical conditions, the membrane potential (ΔΨ) was estimated from the distribution of a fluorescent cationic dye that accumulates in the matrix in proportion to ΔΨ.

Oxygen consumption rates are shown in Table 1 and membrane potentials in Figure 1. In fresh mitochondria, 40 nmol of O₂ was consumed during the state 3 interval in which the 200 nmol of ADP was phosphorylated. The respiratory control ratio, defined as the state 3 rate divided by the state 4 rate, was 5.7 for fresh mitochondria and 1.8 for stored mitochondria. The investigators concluded that storage had impaired the coupling of respiration to phosphorylation, and they set out to identify which component of the system was responsible.

figures.caption: Table 1 Oxygen consumption after each sequential addition (nmol O₂/min/mg protein; means of n = 4 preparations, SD within 10% of each mean)
Figure 1 Membrane potential (ΔΨ, matrix negative) after each sequential addition, estimated from dye distribution (mean ± SD, n = 4)

source: Data are illustrative, constructed for practice.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, what is the ADP/O ratio (ADP phosphorylated per oxygen atom reduced) of the fresh mitochondria oxidizing glutamate and malate?
why: Wrong: 0.4 is 80 nmol O ÷ 200 nmol ADP, the ratio inverted (oxygen atoms per ADP rather than ADP per oxygen atom).
Right: 40 nmol O₂ is 80 nmol of oxygen atoms, and 200 nmol ADP ÷ 80 nmol O = 2.5, close to the modern value for NADH-linked substrates.
Wrong: 3.0 is the classic textbook P/O for NADH, recalled rather than calculated from the passage's numbers.
Wrong: 5.0 is 200 ÷ 40, which divides by molecules of O₂ rather than by oxygen atoms.

questions.stem: According to Table 1, about how much of the oxygen consumption of fresh mitochondria after oligomycin addition is due to electron transport through the respiratory chain?
why: Wrong: 2 nmol O₂/min/mg is the rate that survives antimycin A, which is O₂ use that does not pass through the electron transport chain.
Right: subtracting the antimycin-insensitive rate, which does not pass through the chain, gives 9 − 2 = 7 nmol O₂/min/mg.
Wrong: 9 nmol O₂/min/mg is the whole oligomycin rate, which still includes the 2 nmol O₂/min/mg that is not mitochondrial respiration.
Wrong: 13 is the state 4 rate minus the antimycin rate; it describes the system before oligomycin was added, not after.

questions.stem: A reviewer proposes that storage lowered the respiratory control ratio by making the inner membrane leakier to protons, not by reducing ATP synthase activity. Which comparison in Table 1 tests this proposal most directly?
choices: The fresh and stored rates after oligomycin
The fresh and stored rates in state 3
The fresh and stored rates after antimycin A
The fresh and stored rates after FCCP
why: Right: With Fo blocked, respiration can only replace protons that leak back across the membrane. A rise from 9 to 33 nmol O₂/min/mg points to more leak, and less ATP synthase activity could not raise this rate.
Wrong: A lower state 3 rate would follow from either a leakier membrane or a weaker ATP synthase, so this comparison cannot tell the two explanations apart.
Wrong: The antimycin rates are identical in both preparations and measure non-mitochondrial O₂ use, which bears on neither explanation.
Wrong: FCCP rates measure how fast the chain can run with no gradient. They are similar in the two preparations and say nothing about membrane leak versus synthase activity.

questions.stem: If the fresh mitochondria were given succinate plus rotenone instead of glutamate and malate, how would the measured ADP/O ratio most likely change?
choices: It would rise, because succinate electrons pass all three proton-pumping complexes
It would not change, because ATP synthase needs the same protons for each ATP
It would fall, because succinate oxidation uses ATP before the chain can be fed
It would fall, because succinate electrons enter at ubiquinone and skip Complex I
why: Wrong: Succinate electrons enter through Complex II, which pumps no protons, and so they pass only Complexes III and IV, not all three pumps.
Wrong: The protons needed per ATP stay the same, but fewer protons are pumped per oxygen atom reduced, so ATP made per O falls.
Wrong: Succinate dehydrogenase does not consume ATP. The direction is right, but the reason is wrong: the ratio falls because Complex II pumps no protons.
Right: Complex II feeds electrons to ubiquinone below Complex I, so each pair pumps about 6 rather than 10 protons and the ADP/O falls from about 2.5 to about 1.5.

questions.stem: In fresh mitochondria, adding ADP raised O₂ consumption (Table 1) while slightly lowering ΔΨ (Figure 1). Which explanation best accounts for both observations?
choices: A larger ΔΨ in state 3 pushes protons through the pumps faster, raising O₂ use
Phosphorylating ADP releases extra electrons into the chain, raising flow to O₂
Protons returning through ATP synthase lower back-pressure, so the pumps speed up
ADP acts like FCCP, carrying protons across the membrane and draining the gradient
why: Wrong: ΔΨ is smaller in state 3 than in state 2 or state 4, and a larger gradient would slow the pumps rather than speed them up. This reverses the relationship.
Wrong: Phosphorylation of ADP neither donates nor releases electrons. Electrons come from NADH made by oxidizing the substrates.
Right: ATP synthase lets protons flow back into the matrix, which partly drains the gradient. With less opposing ΔΨ, the pumps and electron flow to O₂ speed up. This is respiratory control.
Wrong: An FCCP-like effect would collapse ΔΨ to about 25 mV and could not be stopped by oligomycin. ADP lowers ΔΨ only a little, and its effect ends once ADP is used up.
